conceptTag: First customers for a catering business
readerTitle: The caterer with a great menu and no customers
caseNote: 가상 사례 (오피스 케이터링 창업자, 회사 내 시설팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 첫 고객은 기다려서 오는 것이 아니라 고르는 것이다. 좁은 한 무리를 직접 찾아가고, 첫 거래의 할인은 공짜로 주지 말고 약속과 소개와 바꾼다.
misconception: 좋은 메뉴와 웹사이트가 있으면 고객은 알아서 온다. 처음엔 누구든 받고, 깎아 달라면 깎아 줘야 한다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 SAL-06-02 (첫 10명의 고객), SAL-06-05 (첫 거래 가격)
모든 인물과 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 계산 확인: 1인당 $15 × 20명 = 주당 $300. 영구 30% 할인 시 주당 $210, 주당 손실 $90. 12주 손실 $90 × 12 = $1,080. 첫 점심 1회만 30% 할인 시 손실 $90 1회.
모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치이며 실제 케이터링 업계 평균 가격을 뜻하지 않습니다. 게시 전 카드 문구에 업계 통계처럼 읽히는 표현이 없는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: A great menu, a nice website, zero orders.
body: Maya rents time in a shared commercial kitchen. She has a tested lunch menu, food photos and a booking page.
A month in, she has catered one birthday party for a friend. The phone isn't ringing. A website is a shop window, and nobody is walking past it yet.

image.label: A caterer waiting beside trays of food and a silent phone
image.brief: 공유 주방에서 앞치마를 두른 창업자가 잘 차린 도시락 트레이 옆에 서서 조용한 휴대폰을 바라보는 장면. 노트북 화면에는 예약 페이지와 '0 orders'. 따뜻한 색감, 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Where should Maya find her first ten customers?
body: She has time, a small budget and capacity for about five events a week. Which plan gives her the best start?

options.text: Say yes to everyone: weddings, birthdays, offices, schools
options.feedback: She gets variety but no pattern. Each job needs different menus, staff and selling, and no customer can vouch for her to the next.

options.text: List 30 offices within 15 minutes that hold regular team lunches, and visit them herself
options.feedback: This is **your first 10 customers** at work: one narrow, reachable group with the same need, who repeat and talk to each other.

options.text: Spend the budget on online ads aimed at local businesses
options.feedback: Ads may bring a few orders. But she learns little about why people buy, and the budget runs out before a pattern appears.

cards.title: One kind of customer, many times over.
body: Maya drops a small tasting box at each office with a note for whoever orders the food. She learns the buyer is usually an office manager, not the boss.

Their worries are the same everywhere: clear allergy labels, arriving on time, one simple invoice. Because every customer is alike, each lunch makes the next pitch sharper. And office managers in the same building talk at the coffee machine.

image.label: Tasting boxes delivered to office reception desks on one street
image.brief: 지도처럼 내려다본 한 동네 거리. 반경 15분 원 안의 사무실 건물 여러 채에 작은 시식 박스 아이콘. 몇 곳은 체크 표시. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.softwareNote: A software founder can do the same: pick one narrow group of users with the same problem, reach them directly, and let each conversation sharpen the next.

cards.title: "You're new. Can you do 30% off?"
body: An office manager loves the tasting. She wants a weekly lunch for 20 people. Maya's price is $15 a person. Then she asks for 30% off.

options.text: Agree. Landing the first regular client matters most
options.feedback: She wins the client but sets $10.50 as the real price. Raising it later feels like a betrayal.

options.text: Keep $15, but take 30% off the first lunch in exchange for four booked weeks and two introductions
options.feedback: This is **pricing your first deals**: a discount is never free. It buys a commitment and referrals, and the price stays honest.

options.text: Offer the first month free to prove the quality
options.feedback: It removes the risk for the client, but it tests whether people like free food, not whether they'll pay.

cards.title: Two ways to give 30% off.
body: Same discount, very different cost. Over 12 weeks, the permanent cut costs twelve times more and buys nothing back.

breakdown.label: 30% off the first lunch only
breakdown.detail: Paid once, traded for 4 weeks and 2 referrals

cards.title: Narrow is a starting point, not a cage.
body: Focusing on office lunches means Maya depends on one kind of demand. If offices move to more remote days, her orders shrink together.

Her first ten customers are for learning and references, not her whole future market. Once offices run smoothly, she can test a second group, such as office parties. And holding her price only works if the food and delivery earn it every week.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a large company.
body: You run the facilities team at a company with 40 departments. You've launched a healthier meeting-lunch service, billed to each department's budget. Nobody has used it yet.
How do you win your first internal customers?

options.text: Email all 40 departments with the menu and a booking link
options.feedback: Everyone hears about it, but an email is a website in disguise. Few act, and you learn little about why.

options.text: Pick four departments that hold frequent meetings and dislike the current food, and meet their managers
options.feedback: This is **your first 10 customers** again: a small, similar group you can reach, serve well and turn into internal references.

options.text: Ask leadership to make the service mandatory
options.feedback: Usage jumps, but you never learn whether teams value it, and resentment grows if the food disappoints.

cards.softwareNote: The same holds for an internal software tool: a few teams who chose it beat forty who were told to use it.

cards.title: Choose your first customers, then make every discount buy something.
body: Concepts used: **your first 10 customers** (a narrow, reachable group you go to yourself) and **pricing your first deals** (keep the real price, trade any discount for commitment or referrals).
**Try it today:** write down the one group your next ten customers should come from, and one thing you'd ask for in return for a discount.

image.label: Ten place settings at one table, each with a name card
image.brief: 긴 테이블 하나에 비슷한 사무실 직원 열 명분의 자리. 각 자리에 이름표와 도시락. 한쪽에 '$15' 가격표가 그대로 붙어 있음. 실제 로고 없음.
